title: camcraft-mcp skill: 8 tools' arguments don't match the server (post path vs output, add_operation model vs source, ...)
body:
The `camcraft-mcp` skill's tool reference (`.claude/skills/camcraft-mcp/SKILL.md`) gives argument names that the server refuses for 8 tools. An agent that follows the skill gets `unknown argument` errors on its first job.

**Compared against `tools/list` from `camcraft-cli mcp` at `main` f42d3788:**

| Tool | Skill says | Server takes (required in bold) | Server reply to the skill's shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| `post` | `post?`, `path?` | **`output`**, `post` | `post: unknown argument "path"` |
| `add_operation` | `kind`, `name`, `tool`, `model?`, `params?` | **`kind`**, **`tool`**, `name`, `params`, `source` (`"stock"` or a model name) | `add_operation: unknown argument "model"` |
| `set_stock` | `{ "kind": "box", "box": [x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1] }`, `{ "kind": "model", "model": … }` | `box: {dx, dy, dz}`, `cylinder`, `from_model` | not tried |
| `set_operation_area` | `name`, `containment`, `offset?` | **`operation`**, **`area`** (an object: `offset`, `corner`, …) | not tried |
| `set_operation_geometry` | `name`, `picks` | **`operation`**, **`picks`** | not tried |
| `set_work_offset` | `offset`, `setup?` | **`word`**, `setup` | not tried |
| `load_machine` | `name?`, `setup?` | `builtin`, `path`, `clear`, `setup` | not tried |
| `add_tool` | `name`, … ("from catalog name") | `catalog`, `definition`, `name` | not tried |

The first two refusals were met while driving a job by the skill. The rest come from comparing the skill's signatures with the `inputSchema` of each tool. The in-repo tests use the server's names (`crates/app/tests/mcp*.rs`: `"output"`, `"source"`, `{"box": {"dx": …}}`, `"operation"`), so the skill is the side that drifted.

**Also stale in the same file:** "Known Remaining Gaps" items 2 (setup alignment, now `set_part_axes`) and 6 (pocket recognition, now `detect_pockets`) have shipped. Items 1 (`MoveModel`) and 3 (`RepairModel`) are open PRs #719 and #721.

**Neighbour that works:** the signatures for `import_model`, `set_wcs`, `move_fixture`, `add_setup`, `edit_operation`, `set_tool`, `detect_holes`, `render_stock`, `generate` and `verify` match the server.

**Done means:**
- The 8 entries are corrected and the gap list brought current, with a `PROCESS_VERSION` bump, since the skill is a process file.
- A test keeps the skill and `tools/list` from drifting again, in the spirit of `scripting::the_bindings_file_is_the_verb_table`. For every `` `name { … }` `` signature in the skill, the tool exists, each documented key is in its `inputSchema` properties, and every required key is documented.

title: fixture_library test fails on Windows: Unix-style paths aren't absolute there

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
What happens: the batch tier on main (f42d3788, Windows) is red on one test. It is `crates/app/tests/fixture_library.rs`, `the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines` (1635 passed, 1 failed). Every other lane is green, clippy included.

```
panicked at crates\app\tests\fixture_library.rs:117:5:
  left: None
 right: Some("/shop/fixtures")
```

Cause: the test feeds Unix paths (`/shop/fixtures`, `/Users/me`) to `fixture_library::user_dir_for("macos", …)`. `crates/app/src/fixture_library/store.rs:32` keeps an override only if `PathBuf::is_absolute()`, and that test runs on the host OS. On Windows `/shop/fixtures` has no drive letter, so it isn't absolute and is dropped. The test likely passes on Linux and macOS.

Came from: a3c859bd (fixture library, #339), merged via d0f0a80b. Nothing has touched the file since.

Fix options: make the test's paths host-absolute (built from `std::env::temp_dir()` or `cfg!(windows)` pairs), or have `user_dir_for` judge absoluteness by the target OS string it is given, not by the host. Check how the machine-library sibling (`user_dir_for` there, if any) handles it and match it.

Done means: `fixture_library` passes on Windows and the batch tier is green on main.

title: MCP verify says ok: true while the ops' own warnings block the post
body:
`verify` answers `"ok": true` for a program that `post` then refuses, when the refusal comes from an op's own warnings. The findings in the same reply say `"blocks_post": true`; only the summary flag is wrong.

**Reproduction** (`main` f42d3788, `camcraft-cli mcp`, Windows):

```
import_model   {"path": "tall.stl"}          (a 40 x 40 x 30 box, z 0..30)
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 60, "dy": 60, "dz": 30}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0400-2FL"}     (Ø4 cutter, 12 mm flutes, Ø6 shank)
add_operation  {"kind": "contour", "tool": "EM-0400-2FL", "name": "C1", "source": "tall"}
generate {}    -> C1 ok
verify {}      -> "ok": true, "gate": {"ok": true, "problems": []},
                  84 findings, all {"kind": "shank_hit", "blocks_post": true}
post           {"post": "Fanuc", "output": "tall.nc"}
               -> post blocked - 84 warning(s): C1: shank/holder at move 48 collides with the part or an island; ...
```

The 84 hits are real: the Ø6 shank rides a 30 mm wall the Ø4 cutter is contouring, below its 12 mm flutes. The same mismatch shows on a 3D Finish over `testdata/models/Milling-test.step` with `BN-0600`: `ok: true`, 3232 blocking `shank_hit` findings, post refused.

**Neighbour cases that agree:**
- When the program gate has a problem (for example a gouge), `ok` is `false` and the post is refused.
- With no findings, `ok` is `true` and the post writes.

**Root cause (confirmed):** `v_verify` (`crates/app/src/script/api.rs:184-185`) computes `ok = ops_ok && fresh && gate.ok`, and `ops_ok` reads each op's generation status (`ok` / `stale` / `never`), never its warnings. The post holds on exactly those warnings: `posting::stream_records` turns every cached warning with `blocks_post()` into a `WARN` record for each non-suppressed op, and `post_script_body` refuses on any engine warning (`crates/app/src/posting.rs:405`). The doc comment on `v_check` says it is the verify "the way the post gate reads it: one judgment". The MCP `verify` and the script API's `cam.check()` both go through `v_verify`.

**Why it matters:**
- An agent or script that checks `ok` before posting is told the program is clean, then gets a refusal it wasn't warned about.
- The batch CLI's exit code reads the same flag (`crates/app/src/cli.rs`, `report`). With the project above saved as `tall.camproj`:
  - `camcraft-cli process tall.camproj` exits **0**, "clean".
  - `camcraft-cli process tall.camproj -o tall.nc` exits 1 with `post blocked - 84 warning(s)`.

  So a CI job that only verifies passes a program that can't be posted.

**Done means:**
- `ok` is `false` when an in-scope, non-suppressed op holds a warning that `blocks_post()`. That is the post's own rule, so a Scallop or ProbeSearch note alone doesn't flip it.
- The reply names which ops hold the post.
- An MCP test pins it with the box-and-contour case above, plus a clean neighbour that stays `ok`.

title: Pocket recognition reads an inside-out mesh as a part-sized pocket (from #512)

labels.name: P0
labels.description: Safety or crash: wrong output, gouge, data loss

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
**Pocket recognition reads an inside-out mesh as a pocket the size of the part.** This is on main since #512 merged (head 7e39726). The maintainer's review found it before the merge.

`recognize::pockets_of` (`crates/app/src/recognize/mod.rs`) takes "up" and "leans into" straight from the facet winding. It never asks the body-winding verdict that #387 added (`pick/winding.rs`, `verdict_for` / `refusal`, used by `pick/align.rs`).

**What happens:** a plain 10 mm cube with every facet reversed returns `Ok([Pocket { kind: Closed, floor_z: 0.0, .. }])`. Its bottom face now "faces up" and its outer walls "lean in", so the part's own outline is reported as a closed pocket as deep as the part. A reversed pocketed block is reported the same way. `detect_pockets` with `create` would then make a Pocket over the part's footprint, cut down to its base: a gouge through the whole part.

**Done means:**
- `pockets_of` runs the winding verdict first and returns its refusal by name, as the pick tools do. A torn or open mesh takes the same route.
- The refusal is pinned by tests with a reversed cube, a reversed pocket block and a torn mesh.

title: MCP: repair an imported model's mesh (RepairModel)
body:
**What's missing:** the GUI's mesh repair, `RepairModel` (`crates/app/src/commands/repair_model.rs`, M13.11), has no MCP tool. The `camcraft-mcp` skill lists it as remaining gap 3. An agent driving `camcraft-cli mcp` that imports an STL with an open edge or near-duplicate vertices can see the damage, but can't fix it headlessly. title: MCP: move and rotate an imported part (MoveModel)
body:
**What's missing:** the GUI's part move/rotate command, `MoveModel` (`crates/app/src/commands/move_model.rs`), has no MCP tool. The `camcraft-mcp` skill lists it as remaining gap 1. Without it, an agent driving `camcraft-cli mcp` can't place an imported part: it can't lift a STEP whose origin sits mid-part so the part's bottom is at Z0, or stand a part up 90°. The workarounds don't cover it:
- `set_wcs` moves the work offset, not the part, so the stock and fixtures stay where they were relative to the model.
- `move_fixture` refuses a part: `'<name>' is not a fixture` (`MoveFixture::new`).

**Neighbour that works:** `move_fixture { name, position, rotation? }` places a fixture through `MoveFixture`, one undo step (`crates/app/src/mcp/fixture_tools.rs`).

**Done means:**
- A `move_model { name, position: [x, y, z], rotation?: [x, y, z, w] }` tool runs `MoveModel::new` through `env.history`, so it is one undo step. An omitted rotation keeps the part's current one.
- It returns the part's new placement and each stock that followed it (stock made from that model, or the stock of a one-part document, as `MoveModel` already moves).
- `MoveModel`'s own refusals come back as tool errors, by name: a fixture, a work offset, the machine table, an unknown name, a non-finite position or a quaternion that doesn't normalize.
- In-process JSON-RPC tests pin all three: a move with its following stock, undo and redo, and the refusals.

title: grblHAL post: 4th axis (rotary A) - indexing and wrapping
body:
### What

The grblHAL post from #710 is 3-axis only: any record carrying a rotary angle is refused by name ("tilted move - grblHAL post has no RTCP output"). grblHAL itself drives extra axes (A/B/C), and common grblHAL boards have 4-5 stepper outputs (e.g. RP2350-based breakouts), so a rotary 4th axis on a router or mill (an A axis with its rotation along X, i.e. a rotary table / indexer) is a realistic setup.

### Scope (to be settled when picked)

- **Indexing (3+2 on one rotary):** position A with `G0 A..`, then mill 3-axis in the rotated frame. Needs: the machine file stating the rotary (axis, travel, resolution), the post writing A words, and the frame transform taken from the stream, never guessed.
- **Rotary wrapping (simultaneous 4th axis):** rotary contour / parallel operations with continuous A. grblHAL has no RTCP/TCPM, so moves must be posted in machine coordinates with inverse-time or per-minute feed handled explicitly. Check against grblHAL's public docs which feed mode it supports (G93?).
- A generic 4-axis grblHAL machine file (`grblhal-4axis.mch`) to pair with it.
- Out of scope: 5-axis simultaneous on grblHAL.

Clean-room as usual: grblHAL's public core README / wiki and the LinuxCNC G-code reference for behaviour only; no GPL source read.

**Done means:** a 4-axis grblHAL machine mounts; a 3+2 indexed operation posts `G0 A..` plus 3-axis moves with goldens; rotary operations either post with a verified feed mode or are refused by name; tilts the machine cannot reach are refused by name; the 3-axis machine still refuses any A word.

Related: #710 (3-axis grblHAL post).

title: grblHAL post processor (3-axis mill)
body:
### What are you trying to do

Post 3-axis milling programs for machines running [grblHAL](https://github.com/grblHAL), the open controller firmware used on many hobby and small-shop routers and mills (RP2040/RP2350, STM32, ESP32, Teensy boards). CamCraft has no grbl-family post yet; the closest is `tormach.cps` (LinuxCNC dialect), but grblHAL understands a smaller subset and posting Tormach output to it fails or misbehaves.

I'm building a grblHAL machine and its sender, so I can test the output against a real controller once it runs, and against grblHAL's simulator before that.

### How you imagine it working

A new `assets/posts/grblhal.cps` (3-axis mill), structured like `tormach.cps` and specced from grblHAL's public documentation and the RS-274/LinuxCNC G-code references (behaviour only; no grblHAL source read, as it is GPL), plus a generic `assets/machines/grblhal-3axis.mch`.

What the post has to respect (each one to be checked against grblHAL's docs while writing it):
- **No cutter compensation**: grblHAL has no G41/G42, so the post always takes CamCraft's computed (in-computer) path and refuses an operation set to control compensation, by name.
- **Tool length**: G43.1 (dynamic tool length offset, Z) by default, with an option for G43 H when the controller has a tool table.
- **Tool change**: `M6 T<n>` on a line of its own, followed by the length offset on the next line (some senders hold the M6 line and drop the rest of it); Z up first.
- **Canned cycles**: G81/G82/G83 (and G73) when enabled in the post's options, otherwise expanded into G0/G1 moves.
- Spindle M3/M4/M5 with S, coolant M7/M8/M9, WCS G54-G59, G90/G94/G17/G21 (or G20), arcs G2/G3 in the XY plane, program end M30, comments in parentheses.

**Done means:** `grblhal.cps` and the machine file ship in `assets/`; the post is in the conformance list and the cross-post tests (`comment_escape`, `control_comp`, `wear_comp`, `comp`) like `tormach`; a `grblhal_post` test and goldens under `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/grblhal/` cover contour, pocket, face, slot, trace, drill, peck and tool change; control compensation is refused with a named reason.

title: Machines: Makera Carvera (C1) and Carvera Air definitions, plus a Carvera post

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Add machine definitions, and the post they need, for Makera's Carvera desktop CNC mills. **There are two models:**

| | Carvera (C1) | Carvera Air |
|---|---|---|
| 3-axis work area | ~360 × 240 × 140 mm | ~300 × 200 × 130 mm |
| 4th axis (optional) | Ø92 × 240 mm | Ø92 × 200 mm |
| Spindle | 200 W, 0–15,000 rpm, closed loop | 200 W, 0–13,000 rpm |
| Tool change | automatic, 6 tools | manual quick-change |
| Probe | wireless probe as T0 | as the C1 |
| Motion | ball screws | 20 mm linear rods, ball screws |

The figures are from Makera's product pages and retailer listings. Confirm each against Makera's official spec sheet or manual before committing a `.mch` (see Done means). One retailer listing (280 × 120 × 60 mm, 30k rpm, 5 tools) describes some other machine, so ignore it.

**Controller:** both run Makera's Smoothieware-based firmware ([supported codes](https://wiki.makera.com/en/supported-codes)), driven over USB or Wi-Fi by Carvera Controller, with the program running on the controller.

**Post requirements** (from Makera's supported-codes page and the community firmware docs):
- **Tool change:** `M6 Tn` is an automatic tool change on the C1. `T0` is the wireless probe and `T-1` means no tool.
  - The Air's changer is manual, so a tool change prompts the operator in Controller.
  - Community firmware 2.1.0c adds custom tool slots and manual-change prompts on the C1 for tools above 6. The post must state which tool numbers the C1's changer holds, and treat the rest as manual.
- **Dialect:** the firmware is not Fanuc or LinuxCNC. The post emits only words on the supported-codes list, and anything else (canned cycles it doesn't list, G43 behaviour, comments) is checked against that list and refused by name.
- **Rotary:** the 4th axis is an A-axis rotary along X, with its own travel and speed limits.

**Done means:**
- `assets/machines/makera-carvera.mch` and `makera-carvera-air.mch` exist, with travels, spindle range and power, axis speeds and the rotary option. Every figure is sourced from Makera's spec sheet or manual and cited in the decision file.
- Both are registered in `posting::MACHINES`, with tests in the style of the Tormach machine tests.
- A Carvera post exists: the tool-change and probe behaviour above, refusals by name for codes the firmware doesn't support, and a golden `.nc` for a small pocket with a tool change.
- A Carvera Controller or real-machine run is requested from a contributor with the machine before the post is trusted.

title: Mill generators can lose their approach rapid when the start point is exactly X0 Y0

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Follow-up from #690 / PR #694 (review note).

Most mill generators start their `PathBuilder` cursor at (0, 0, clearance) and open with a rapid to their start point on the clearance plane. That rapid is the program's approach: posts write only a move's end point, so it becomes the `G00` after the tool call.

`PathBuilder::push` drops a zero-length move. When a generator's start point is exactly X0 Y0, the approach rapid therefore disappears. The first posted motion is then whatever follows, typically a plunge or ramp feed from the tool-change position. That is #690's bug, reached through a different door.

#694 closed this for Face by stating a zero-length rapid when the path doesn't open with one. The others are unchecked, including chamfer, the finishing3d family (raster, flat, pencil, polar, morph, flow, shadow, rings, geodesic, deburr) and the 2D ladders.

**Done means:**
- Each generator that seeds its cursor at (0, 0, clearance) is checked with a fixture whose start is exactly X0 Y0.
- Any that lose the approach are fixed. A shared rule is preferred, for example a `PathBuilder` or `Toolpath` helper that guarantees the first move is a rapid at clearance, over per-generator patches.
- A test pins that the first move is a rapid for each affected generator.

Related: #690, PR #694

title: main: probe_tormach goldens are stale after #579 and #583 merged together (6/7 fail)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
`cargo test -p camcraft-app --test probe_tormach` fails 6 of 7 on upstream main (seen while gating #694 after merging upstream/main; that branch touches only Face files):

```
face_posts_g38_2_and_sets_z_on_the_770mx    FAILED  golden nc/tormach/probe_face.nc is stale
edge_ / bore_ / corner_ / boss_ ..._on_the_770mx, bore_posts_in_mm_on_a_metric_machine   FAILED (same)
```

**Cause:** two PRs merged cleanly in text but not in meaning, two minutes apart:
- #579 (#570, merged 054ecc60) made the probe cycle rapid to the safe plane and *feed* only below it.
- #583 (#575, merged a24ef551) carried Tormach probe goldens written against the cycle from before #570. Those goldens expect a protected `G38.3` descent from Z1.9685 to the safe plane, where the post now writes `G0 ... Z0.9843` and then the probe move.

The new output matches #570's intent: no probe rapid runs below the safe plane, which is Z 25 mm = 0.9843 in for these fixtures. So this looks like stale goldens, not a safety regression. The fix should still read each regenerated `.nc` to confirm that, not just accept the diff.

**Done means:** the `probe_tormach` goldens are regenerated on a branch (`WRITE_GOLDEN=1`), the diff is read line by line against #570's rule, and the suite passes on main.

title: Picking: only feature edges, feature points and faces are pickable, never tessellation edges or hidden geometry - one rule for the whole app

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10.

## What happens
1. **Tessellation edges are pickable.** The selector lets you pick edges between the mesh's own triangles (at a model's vertices, inside flat faces and along smooth curves). Those aren't real model edges, and no feature should ever be built on them.
2. **Picks go through the model.** In some cases, the "select through" behaviour picks an edge (or a vertex) on the far side of the model, hidden from the user, instead of what's under the cursor.
3. **Inconsistent everywhere.** Face, vertex and edge picking behave differently from page to page: setup alignment, operation geometry, fixture mates, the WCS/origin picks, MCP picks. Users can't build a mental model of what a click will select.

## What should happen - one picking rule, used everywhere
- **Faces:** a face is a welded face, i.e. a smooth patch of triangles merged across soft edges (the `features`/`area` patches MCP's `list_features` already reports). Clicking anywhere on it picks the whole face, never a single triangle.
- **Edges:** only **feature edges** are pickable: edges where two welded faces meet at a real crease, plus open boundary edges of a sheet. Edges between triangles of the same welded face (flat-face triangulation, facets of a smooth cylinder) are never pickable. Chains follow feature edges only.
- **Points:** only **feature points** are pickable: corners where feature edges meet, the end points of open feature-edge chains, and (where a mode asks for it) arc/circle centres derived from a round feature edge. Interior mesh vertices are never pickable.
- **Visible first, never through:** a pick resolves to the front-most visible surface under the cursor (the same depth the viewport draws, perspective and ortho). An edge or point is pickable only if it is visible there (not occluded by the model, within a small screen-space tolerance of the front surface). Nothing on the far side is picked unless the user explicitly turns on a "pick through" mode, which is off by default and shown as such.
- **Snapping order near a feature:** within the pick radius, prefer point, then edge, then face, but **only** among the kinds the current tool accepts (e.g. plane alignment is faces only after #554; axis by edge or two points takes edges/points). A tool that doesn't accept edges never snaps to one.
- **One implementation:** a single picking service in the app layer (feature graph: welded faces, feature edges, feature points; visibility test against the depth the viewport uses) that every UI picker (`plane_pick`, `edge_pick`, `vertex_pick`, `axis_pick`, fixture locate, origin/WCS picks) and the MCP pick tools call. No page carries its own picking rules.

## Done means
- A shared feature-graph and pick API in the app layer, with tests:
  - a flat face's triangulation edges are not pickable;
  - a cylinder's facet edges are not pickable but its circular rim is;
  - a box corner is a pickable point, while a vertex inside a face isn't;
  - a feature edge on the far side of the part is not picked through the near face, in both perspective and ortho;
  - "pick through", when explicitly on, does pick it.
- Every UI picker and the MCP pick tools use it (no local pick logic left); UI tests on the setup page, op geometry and fixture locate confirm the behaviour.
- A short note in the user docs (#688) on what a click picks.

Related: #554 (plane picks faces only), #557 (axis by edge/points), #555 (three points), #561/#566 (fixture locate), #180 (MCP picks), #241 (selecting on complex planar faces), #613/#609/#610 (ortho rays).

**Reproduction** (main b57f8d52, Windows, `camcraft-cli mcp`):

```
set_stock      {"box":{"dx":10,"dy":10,"dz":10}}
add_tool       {"catalog":"EM-0600-4FL"}
add_operation  {"kind":"face","tool":"EM-0600-4FL","name":"X","params":{"stepover":1e-9}}   -> ok, status never
generate       {"name":"X"}
```

After about 113 s the server dies without a reply:

```
memory allocation of 95999996328 bytes failed
```

Same with a 2D Contour, `{"stepdown":1e-9}`, on a 1 mm cube model (`testdata/models/cube_inside_out.stl`). After about 197 s:

```
memory allocation of 137438953472 bytes failed
```

Not tried in the GUI.

**Neighbour cases that still work:**
- `stepover` 0 or -1 is refused at `add_operation`: `operation parameters are not usable for a Face operation`.
- A 2D Pocket with `stepover` 1000 is refused by name at generate: `stepover leaves bands the tool cannot reach`.

**Root cause (confirmed):** nothing bounds the number of passes or levels.
- `OpParams::is_sane` (`crates/app/src/operation/types/sane.rs`) only asks `pos(x)`, finite and above 0.
- The facer's row builder `band` (`crates/motion/src/machining2d/face.rs`) and the depth ladder `cut_levels` (`crates/motion/src/machining2d/levels.rs`) push one row or level per step until they reach the far side. Neither has a count cap.
- A 1e-9 mm step over a few mm asks for about 10^10 entries, and the allocation failure aborts the process.
- If a step is ever below the ULP of the coordinate (`y + step == y`), the loop never advances and grows until memory runs out.

Done means:
- a stepover or stepdown that would produce more passes than a named maximum is refused by name, either at command creation or at generate, instead of running;
- a normal small value (for example 0.05 mm) still generates;
- both are pinned by tests on Face and on a depth-stepping op.

title: Face posts no approach rapid: the first motion after the tool call is a 3-axis feed from the tool-change position to cutting depth
body:
A Face operation's posted program has no approach rapid. The first motion after the tool call is a **3-axis feed from wherever the tool change left the spindle, straight to cutting depth**. Every other mill op opens with a `G00` to its start point on the clearance plane.

**Reproduction** (main b57f8d52, `camcraft-cli mcp`):

```
set_stock      {"box":{"dx":40,"dy":30,"dz":10}}
add_tool       {"catalog":"EM-0600-4FL"}
add_operation  {"kind":"face","tool":"EM-0600-4FL","name":"F1","params":{"cut_z":{"offset":-0.5,"reference":"top_of_stock"}}}
generate {}    -> ok
verify {}      -> gate ok, 0 findings
post           {"output":"...","post":"Fanuc"}
```

```
T02 M6
G43 H02
S9500 M3
M8
G01 X-23 Y-12 Z9.5 F300      <- first motion: XYZ together, at plunge feed, from the tool-change position
G01 X23 Y-12 Z9.5 F1200
...
G00 X23 Y12 Z35
```

Haas, Siemens 840D, Heidenhain and Mazak post the same first line. The committed goldens show it in every dialect: `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/face_square_40x40.nc` line 5, `G01 X-5 Y5 Z-2 F100`, and the same line in `haas/`, `heidenhain/`, `mazak/`, `sinumerik/`, `tormach/`.

**Neighbour case that works:** every other mill golden's first motion is a rapid to its start: `contour_plate_with_hole.nc` `G00 X37.711 Y-6.306 Z5`, `pocket_zigzag_plate_with_island.nc` `G00 X4.5 Y4.6 Z5`, `drill_plate.nc` `G00 X10 Y10 Z0`, `slot_wide_channel_rows.nc` `G00 X-10 Y-7 Z5`. The other Face golden, `face_square_40x40_stepped.nc`, has the same gap (`G01 X-5 Y5 Z2 F100`).

**Root cause (confirmed):** the facer's path begins at its plunge point. `crates/motion/src/machining2d/face.rs` starts its builder at `PathBuilder::new(Point3::new(entry, ys[0], p.clearance_z))`, so the path's first move is the Plunge (`face_square_40x40.cl`: `START -5000 5000 5000`, then `Plunge -5000 5000 -2000`). The posts write moves, not the path's start point, so the move to the start is never posted. The other mill kernels start at `(0, 0, clearance)`, as noted in `docs/decisions/632-facing-approach.md`, and open with a Rapid to their start. #632 fixed the same gap for lathe facing.

**Why it matters:**
- The machine does a slow diagonal feed from the tool-change position down to the cut, which is not the program that was verified. Verify judged a vertical plunge from `START` on the clearance plane. The posted line ends at cutting depth from an XY and Z the verifier never saw.
- At F300 from a tool-change height several hundred mm up, the approach takes minutes.

Done means: a Face op's posted program reaches its first plunge via a rapid to the start point on the clearance plane in every mill dialect, pinned by the face goldens and a test asserting the first motion after the tool call is a rapid.

title: Post gate refuses a Bore at a STEP hole's own size: the sim charges the 0.02 mm facet sagitta as a 20 mm gouge
body:
A Bore on a modelled hole, at the hole's own size, is refused by the post gate as a **20 mm gouge**. The operation's own verify finds nothing. The overcut being charged is the gap between the true circle the bore cuts and the inscribed facets of the imported mesh, about 0.02 mm sideways.

**Reproduction** (main b57f8d52, Windows, `camcraft-cli mcp`):

```
import_model   {"path":"testdata/models/Milling-test.step","name":"part"}
set_stock      {"from_model":"part"}
add_tool       {"catalog":"EM-1000-4FL"}
add_operation  {"kind":"bore","tool":"EM-1000-4FL","source":"part","name":"OP"}
detect_holes   {"name":"OP"}        -> 1 hole: xy (0, 0), radius 12.5, entry z 20, floor z 0
generate       {"name":"OP"}        -> status ok, 0 warnings
verify         {}
```

`verify` returns no per-op finding. The program gate says:

```
gouge: program cuts below the model in 1 cell(s), worst 20.00 mm at (4.69, 11.59, z 0.00)
```

(4.69, 11.59) is at r = 12.50, on the hole wall. The same happens with EM-0800-4FL (1 cell, 20.00 mm at (11.76, -4.23)) and EM-0600-4FL (4 cells, 20.00 mm at (9.57, -8.04)).

**Neighbour cases that still work:**
- The same bore with `"stock_to_leave": 0.01` verifies clean, and so do 0.015, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. With 0.005 it is still refused.
- A 2D Contour around the part's outside (convex walls) on the same finished-part setup passes the gate.

**Root cause (likely):** the STEP mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict.
- `list_features` on the part shows the Ø25 hole wall as 53 flat strips, 6.79° each. The chord sagitta is 12.5 × (1 − cos 3.40°) = **0.022 mm**.
- The STEP importer meshes to a chord tolerance of `extent * 1e-3` (`crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs`, `tol_target`), about 0.06 mm for this 60 mm part.
- The program sim judges against those facets with `tol` = `GOUGE_TOL` = 0.01 mm (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/deviate.rs`, `deviate`). The sideways slack from #299 (`wall_slack.rs`) is the same 0.01 mm.
- On a concave curved wall the facets lie inside the true surface. A bore that cuts the true r = 12.5 therefore removes up to 0.022 mm of "model" between chord and arc. That is past the 0.01 slack, so the column is charged the wall's full 20 mm height.

The sagitta (0.022) against the threshold (stock_to_leave 0.01 plus tol 0.01) matches where the refusal stops. That is why this says "likely" and not "confirmed".

Any finishing pass that meets a concave curved wall at nominal size should hit the same thing: bores, a contour inside a round boss pocket, round internal corners. A larger part has a coarser mesh (extent/1000), so its sagitta is larger.

Done means: a bore at a STEP hole's nominal size verifies clean, a bore 0.05 mm oversize into the same wall is still refused, and both are pinned by tests.

title: Documentation and a browser build of CamCraft on GitHub Pages, built with Zola at each release

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Proposed by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10. **Paused (`P?`) for the maintainer's review**; nothing is picked up until he sets a priority.

## Goal
A public site on GitHub Pages with:
1. **Documentation** (user guide plus developer and architecture docs), generated with **[Zola](https://www.getzola.org/)** (a single binary static site generator, Markdown content, Tera templates, no Node toolchain).
2. **CamCraft in the browser:** the WASM build of the app, published alongside the docs, so a release can be tried without installing anything.

## How it should work
- **Source:** a Zola project in the repo (e.g. `site/`: `config.toml`, `content/`, `templates/`, `static/`). The docs content lives there as Markdown. Existing material is reused where it fits (README sections, `docs/` design notes, release notes).
- **Output folder:** Zola builds into one folder that Pages picks up. Options to decide in review: the `public/` output deployed by the Pages "GitHub Actions" source, or a `gh-pages` branch / `docs/` folder. The site is **regenerated from scratch each release** (no incremental state, no hand-edited output in git).
- **Part of the release cycle:** generating and publishing the site is a step of the minor/major cut (AGENTS.md "A cut goes PR review -> merge to main -> tag"), run on the tagged tree. If it runs on GitHub, it goes in the existing tag-triggered `release.yml`. **No new `push`/`pull_request`/`schedule` trigger** (AGENTS.md Actions budget). It can also be built locally (`zola build`) for previews.
- **Versioned content:** the site shows the version it was built from. Each release overwrites the previous site (one live version); older versions stay in the GitHub releases.
- **WASM app:** the release step builds the app for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (the web build from #31), bundles it (e.g. `wasm-bindgen` + a small loader page, or `trunk`), and places it under the site (e.g. `/app/`), so `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/app/` runs CamCraft in the browser. It is linked from the docs front page with a note on what works in the browser and what doesn't (file access, GPU features).

## Open questions (for the review)
- Pages source: Actions-deployed `public/` vs a branch/folder? (Actions deploy keeps generated files out of git.)
- WASM readiness: #31 says only geometry, CL and post build for wasm32 today. Does this issue wait for #31, or ship docs first and add `/app/` when #31 lands?
- Content scope for the first cut: user guide only, or the developer/architecture section too?
- Relation to #291 (needs-research, which proposed mdBook): this issue picks Zola. On approval, #291's research is folded in here, or #291 is closed as superseded.
- Actions minutes: building the WASM app and the site on the tag run adds billed minutes. Measure and keep it within the budget.

## Done means (once approved and broken down)
- A Zola site in the repo builds locally with `zola build`.
- The release cycle regenerates and publishes it to GitHub Pages at each minor/major cut, with no new CI triggers.
- The published site carries the version and links to the release downloads.
- The WASM build of CamCraft is published under the site and loads in a current browser (once #31 makes the UI build for wasm32).
- AGENTS.md's release steps name the site step.

Related: #291 (documentation site, mdBook proposal), #31 (app and UI on wasm), #72 (release compile targets).

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

title: Refusals name their spot: adopt GenError::invalid_at at the remaining located refusal sites (#261 follow-up)
body:
Follow-up to #261 part 2 (PR forthcoming from `vilts:issue/261-refused-location`).

**Today (with that PR):** a generator refusal can name the spot it is about (`GenError::invalid_at(msg, spot)` → `CommandError::MachiningAt`). The viewport marks that spot and the op page's refusal line frames it. Only the first adopters do so: Face's narrow strip between two holes, the drill cycle's R-plane / counterbore / bore-fit / centre-cutting doors, Bore's and Thread's counterbore and fit doors, and the plunge law. The other roughly 620 `GenError::Invalid` / `Empty` sites name no spot. Their refusal shows text only, as before.

**Expected:** every refusal that is about one place on the part names it. Candidates found by a grep for coordinates in the refusal text:
- app: `operation/cross_part.rs`, `cross_stock.rs`, `drill_reach.rs` (2 sites), `drill_top.rs`, `rotary_gate.rs` (2), `stitch_cross.rs`
- motion: `drilling/axial.rs` (4), `drilling/cross.rs` (3), `finishing3d/deburr.rs`, `multiaxis/rotary_links.rs`, `turning/bore/mod.rs`, `turning/contour/rides.rs`, `turning/thread.rs`

There may be more whose sentence names a feature rather than a coordinate.

**How:** swap `GenError::Invalid(format!(..))` for `GenError::invalid_at(format!(..), spot)`. The spot must be in the frame the generator runs in, because `run_job` maps it to world. A turning kernel's spot is in its meridian frame, and that frame needs its own mapping first. Any code or test that matches `GenError::Invalid(_)` on an adopted site must also accept `GenError::At { .. }`.

**Done means:** each listed site either names its spot, with a test asserting the world spot, or carries a one-line comment on why it names none (for example a turning meridian with no world mapping yet).

title: Plasma: verification laws for through-cuts - kerf crossing, cut order, rapids, 2D gouge (part of #621)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
**Plasma verification laws: what replaces the gouge and collision checks for a through-cut.**

From [UM10720](https://tormach.com/media/asset/u/m/um10720_1300pl_1223a_web.pdf) §1.4.2, §4.12.8, §4.13 and the LinuxCNC Plasma Primer §12:
- **Kerf crossing.** A cut path that crosses an already-cut kerf or void (THC dives into the gap, which "can smash the torch into the material") is warned, naming the contour and point. A rapid across a cut-out part's area is warned too (tip-up hazard).
- **Cut order.** A part's inner contours must be cut before the outer that frees it. A violation is refused by name.
- **Rapids.** Rapids run at the operator's G30 Z (no CAM Z). The post must emit G30 after every M205; a missing G30 is a post bug that the law catches.
- **Kerf against the part.** The kerf-offset path must not cut into the part's material, which is the 2D gouge (part geometry versus the kerf band).
- **The 3D stock sim** doesn't run for plasma ops. The verdict is the 2D laws above, stated as such and not silently skipped.

**Done means:** each law is pinned with a fixture that trips it and one that passes; the program verdict blocks the post on a refusal (Prime Directive).

body:
**A PathPilot plasma post for the Tormach 1300PL.**

Words from [UM10720](https://tormach.com/media/asset/u/m/um10720_1300pl_1223a_web.pdf) §6–7 and Tormach's [post guidelines](https://knowledgebase.tormach.com/8l/pathpilot-post-processor-guidelines):
- **Preamble:** `G20|G21 / G90 / G64 P<inch> / G17 / G54.. / G43 H1 / G30`. G64 P is always in inches.
- **Per contour:** `G0` to the lead-in start, then `M200` (AutoFS; or M207/M208/M209/M210/M211 plus F when the op states them), `G15` (probe), `G16` (pierce + THC on), the XY `G1`/`G2`/`G3` path, `M205` (torch off and back to G30 Z), `G30`.
- **End:** `G30` then `M30`.
- **Refused by name:** M3/M4/M5/M7/M8/M9, any Z cutting move, G95/G96.
- **M6 conflict:** the manual's example uses `T1 M6`, but the guidelines list M6 as unsupported on plasma. It's resolved by **omitting M6** and noting it, pending a Hub or real-machine run.
- **No program delimiters** (`%`).

**Done means:**
- the post writes the per-contour block exactly;
- refusals are pinned;
- a golden `.nc` exists for a plate with an outer profile and two holes;
- a PathPilot Hub (1300PL) run is requested from the contributor before trusting it on a machine.

title: Plasma: a 2D through-cut profile operation - kerf, leads, cut direction, small holes, inner-first (part of #621)

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
**A plasma profile operation: a 2D through-cut with kerf, leads, cut direction and small-hole rules.**

- **Geometry:** closed or open 2D contours, inner and outer, cut through with no depth stepping.
- **Kerf:** the torch's kerf width, applied in the computer (offset path). An option posts G41/G42 instead, with PathPilot's rule of a straight G1 entry longer than the tool radius ([Tormach post guidelines](https://knowledgebase.tormach.com/8l/pathpilot-post-processor-guidelines)).
- **Direction:** outside contours CW, inside CCW (Hypertherm: the square edge on the part). It's overridable, and the override is stated.
- **Leads:** an arc lead-in and lead-out by default, with lengths as parameters.
  - **Small holes:** for Ø below a threshold (default 32 mm, or under 1.5× thickness), use a perpendicular lead-in from near the centre (≤ the radius), **no lead-out**, an optional overburn, and a 60–70 % feed factor (LinuxCNC Plasma Primer §13). A 1300PL forum report links hole lead-outs to arc loss.
- **Cut order:** inner contours before their outer contour, so a part never drops before its holes are cut.
- **Parameters:** feed is optional, since M200 (AutoFS) sets it on the 1300PL. Pierce height, cut height and delay are optional; when left blank, the controller's AutoFS decides.

**Done means:**
- the op generates offset XY paths with leads in the stated directions, inner first;
- small holes take the hole rule;
- it's undoable through commands and round-trips through the project file;
- golden CL output is pinned for a plate with holes.

**A `plasma` machine kind, and the Tormach 1300PL machine file.**

**The kind.** A `kind: plasma` in the `.mch`:
- **Axes:** X and Y cut; Z is the torch lifter, not a depth axis.
- **No spindle:** no rpm range, no power.
- **Torch:** a torch tool (Tool 1 by convention); a kerf width replaces the tool diameter.
- **Engine behaviour:** the machine check judges XY travel and feed. Z cutting depth and rpm checks don't apply and are skipped, not failed. The stock sim's depth model doesn't fit a through-cut, so plasma ops are judged by the 2D plasma laws (the safety sub-issue) instead.

**The 1300PL**, cited from [UM10720 v1223A](https://tormach.com/media/asset/u/m/um10720_1300pl_1223a_web.pdf) §2 and the 03/24 spec sheet:
- **Travels:** X 48.5 / Y 50 / Z 3.9 in. These are the smaller of the manual's and spec sheet's figures; the conflict is recorded in the decision file.
- **Feeds:** 1000 IPM on X and Y, 120 IPM on Z.
- **Rapid:** none is published, so it's left unstated.
- **Units:** inch.
- **Post:** the PathPilot plasma post (sibling sub-issue).

**Today:** **Open** (project) and **Model** (import) both go straight to the OS file dialog (`rfd::FileDialog` in `crates/ui/src/state.rs`; `actions::open_project` and `actions::open_model_dialog`). Nothing remembers what was opened before.

## Proposed behaviour

1. **Two recent lists,** kept separately: **Recent projects** and **Recent models**. Each is newest first, de-duplicated by canonical path, and capped at **N = 10** by default (configurable in Settings, 0 to turn it off).
2. **Where they show:**
   - the toolbar's **Open** and **Model** buttons get a drop-down (or a split-button arrow) listing the recent files, with "Browse…" at the bottom opening the file dialog as today;
   - the File menu, if there is one, gets "Open Recent" submenus too.
3. **Each entry:** shows the file name, with the full path on hover. An entry whose file no longer exists is shown greyed with "(missing)" and is refused by name if clicked (never a crash). A **Clear recent** item empties the list.
4. **When a file is added:** after a successful open, import or **Save As**. A failed open isn't added.
5. **Storage:**
   - **Where:** a per-user settings file, not the project, in the OS config directory, beside any existing app settings.
   - **Bad input:** a corrupt or unreadable recents file is ignored with a logged diagnostic, never a crash.
   - **Paths:** stored as given (absolute), and nothing is uploaded anywhere.
6. **Not undoable:** opening a recent file is the same command path as opening through the dialog. The recent list itself is app preference state, not document state, so it's outside the command history (AGENTS.md "Everything Is a Command": ephemeral or preference UI state is not undoable).
7. **Unsaved changes:** opening a recent project while the current one has unsaved changes takes the same save-or-discard prompt as **Open** today.

## Done means

- **Lists:** both recent lists appear on the Open and Model buttons, newest first, capped and de-duplicated, with missing files greyed out and refused by name, and Clear recent works.
- **Persistence:** they survive an app restart, and a corrupt recents file starts empty with a logged warning.
- **Tests:**
  - app or UI unit tests for the list logic: add, de-dup, cap, missing file, corrupt file;
  - a UI structural test for the drop-down entries (AccessKit labels).
- No snapshot PNG changes in the PR.

**Today:** the machine travel check compares each move's world X with the lathe's X band. The turning kernels put their radius on the **Y** meridian (a cached facing path is (0, y, z)), so on those paths the X band never sees the turning radius, whether nose centre or control point. **Done means:** a facing path on the Y meridian that runs past the X floor is refused by name. A control point (not the nose centre) at the band edge decides it. Existing lathe goldens and suites stay green.

title: View cube: TOP/BOT clicks snap screen roll to the canonical orientation and spin the part when approached from a yawed near-top view
body:
## Symptom

Arriving at the top view from a yawed approach and clicking TOP on the view cube spins the part on screen instead of just leveling off.

Repro (v0.16.0, default camera):

1. Open a part, `F` to frame all.
2. Right-drag-orbit until the camera is nearly overhead (pitch ~85-89°), yawing until the part sits ~90° rotated on screen (eye standing off toward the part's front rather than its right).
3. Click TOP on the view cube.

Actual: the part visibly rotates on screen (up to 180°) as the view lands.
Expected: the top view comes in at the *nearest* equivalent orientation - the part stays put, the view just levels to the pole.

## Root cause

Face clicks command `Camera::toward(face normal)` (the viewcube's standard-orientation rule). For TOP the normal is `[0,0,1]`, so `toward` computes `yaw = atan2(0,0) = 0`, `pitch = asin(1) = pi/2` (`crates/ui/src/viewport.rs`). At a Z pole the forward vector's x/y components vanish, so `basis_right`'s zero-guard returns literal world +X *whatever the yaw*, and `basis_up = cross(right, fwd)` follows to +Y. Every TOP click therefore lands on exactly one of the infinitely many equivalent overhead orientations - screen right = +X, screen up = +Y - and the approach's roll is discarded.

Approaching the pole at yaw `theta`, the on-screen up direction tends to `-cos(theta), -sin(theta), 0` (the horizontal eye-to-target direction). The canonical pole basis matches that only when the eye approached from the front; from the right side (yaw ~+90°) the click lands 180° rolled, and from yaw ~0 it lands 90° rolled. BOT behaves the same (also `atan2(0,0)`).

## Suggested fix

When `toward` lands exactly on a Z pole (`abs(d.z) = 1`), choose the yaw as the current yaw snapped to the nearest 90°, and let the pole zero-guard evaluate at *that* yaw - `right = (-sin yaw, cos yaw, 0)` - instead of a literal `+X`. Roll stays stable at the chosen yaw (the existing pole law, restated: stable per chosen yaw, and yaw itself becomes snap-to-nearest instead of `atan2`'s 0). Non-pole directions are untouched. The click then rotates the view at most 45° on screen from whatever the user was already looking at.

## Test gap

The behavior is currently pinned by two laws in `law_tests.rs::view_cube_tests` that restate the opposite:

- `toward_turns_the_eye_without_moving_it` asserts a TOP click lands `yaw` at exactly 0.
- `pole_views_hold_a_stable_roll` asserts screen right is exactly `+X` at both poles *for arbitrary starting yaws*.

A change here re-pins both - the roll-stability law survives in its "per chosen yaw" form, and a new pin wants: from a near-pole view at yaw theta, a TOP/BOT click lands at a pole whose on-screen up is within 45 degrees of the pre-click on-screen up (nearest quarter). The decision-doc rationale ("nearest equivalent orientation over canonical roll") belongs in `docs/decisions/`.

title: GPU tests force a software adapter, which macOS lacks: they silently skip (or fail) on every Mac

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Found 2026-11-09 while reviewing the GPU fixes (#604, #613). Every GPU test requests wgpu's **software** adapter:
- `crates/ui/tests/gpu_render.rs:30`, `trace_composite.rs:30`, `trace_parity.rs:25`;
- the headless shell run, `crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell.rs:1565` (`headless_run_succeeds`, and through it the two `*_headless_cli_exit_code_is_zero` tests).

All of them pass `RequestAdapterOptions { force_fallback_adapter: true, .. }`.

**What that does on each platform:**
- **Linux and Windows:** there is a software adapter (lavapipe, WARP), so these tests render.
- **macOS:** Metal has **no software fallback**, so the request always fails ("metal had no fallback adapters"), on every Mac, with a real GPU present.

**Effect on macOS:**
- `gpu_render`, `trace_composite` and `trace_parity` return early from `device_and_queue() -> None` and **pass without rendering**. They are silent skips, so a shader regression can't fail them on a Mac.
- `headless_run_succeeds` and the two headless CLI tests **fail** with "No suitable graphics adapter found". This has been read as "this Mac has no GPU", which is wrong.

**Expected:**
- **Adapter choice:** request the software adapter first (deterministic on CI), and on failure request the platform's default hardware adapter (`force_fallback_adapter: false`, low power). The tests then render on a Mac's real Metal GPU.
- **No silent skips:** a test with no adapter at all prints that it skipped, so a skip is never read as a pass. A deliberate "skip when no adapter" stays possible for headless CI without a GPU.

**Done means:**
- on macOS, `gpu_render` / `trace_composite` / `trace_parity` actually render (each asserts it drew pixels) and `headless_run_succeeds` passes;
- a test that found no adapter says so in its output;
- Linux and Windows still pick the software adapter.

title: Viewport: Orthographic mode blanks the whole model (depth clipped by the WebGPU clip volume)
body:
## What happens

Clicking **Orthographic** in the viewport panel (#455, shipped in v0.16.0) blanks the viewport: the model, the toolpath overlay and the stock raster all disappear, leaving only the background. Flipping back to Perspective brings everything back.

## Reproduction

In the app: open any part, click **Orthographic** beside the Shaded/Wireframe radios - the scene disappears.

Headless, on current main (`66791aa6`): the `tests/gpu_render.rs` harness, the same part as `box_stock_paints_steel_over_background`, the same `test_cam()`, only `projection` flipped:

| projection | solid pixels painted (256x256) |
| --- | --- |
| Perspective | 9,326 |
| Orthographic | 0 |

## Root cause

The ortho branch of `Camera::mvp` (`crates/ui/src/viewport.rs`, lines 1349-1350) maps depth the way OpenGL's `glOrtho` does:

```rust
m[2][2] = 2.0 / (near - far);
m[3][2] = (near + far) / (near - far);
```

which spans NDC z over [-1, +1]. WebGPU's clip volume is `-w <= x, y <= w` and `0 <= z <= w` - depth must land in [0, 1] in clip space. An ortho matrix has `clip.w == 1` (the law tests pin this), so any point with `z_ndc < 0` - every point nearer than `(near + far) / 2` - fails `0 <= z` and is clipped away before rasterization. With `near = 0.1` and `far = 40 * dist`, that midpoint is `20 * dist`, twenty times the orbit distance: everything in view is closer than the cut plane, so the whole model is clipped.

The perspective branch carries the same OpenGL-style depth row, but there `clip.w = eye_z > 0` and `z_clip` stays positive for every eye distance the camera can reach (beyond ~0.2 mm), so perspective survives - it only skews depth precision. Ortho hits the hard clip.

## Suggested fix

Map depth to [0, 1] in the ortho branch instead of [-1, +1]:

```rust
m[2][2] = 1.0 / (near - far);
m[3][2] = near / (near - far);
```

near maps to 0.0, far to 1.0, and ortho depth becomes linear. The x/y rows are already right for WebGPU. The depth attachment clears to 1.0 with `CompareFunction::Less`, so no pipeline change is needed.

## Why the tests missed it

The ortho projection law tests pin the affine row, x/y closure under orbit/zoom/dolly, and `clip.w == 1` - but nothing pins the z row, and `clip_in_front_refuses_behind_eye_points` only checks `w`. Every pixel test in `tests/gpu_render.rs` builds cameras with `..Camera::default()`, which is perspective. A law test on the ortho z span and an ortho pixel test in `gpu_render.rs` would have caught both halves.

title: Errors, warnings and status notes still print millimeters in inch documents
body:
Found while auditing every user-visible string that carries a unit suffix.

**What happens:** the mm/inch choice is a document-level lens (`app::units`,
set from the Stock page), applied at the parameter widgets, the parameter
tables and the post. It is *not* applied to the strings the app says at
itself: refusals, machine-limit warnings, simulation verdicts and status
notices are built with `format!("… {x:.3} mm")` over the raw internal
millimeter value. In an inch document every one of those sentences reads in
millimeters, with the internal number, so it cannot be read against the inch
values the user typed a screen earlier.

**Confirmed on `main` b6516886**, by reading the string builders:

- app refusal - `commands/set_stock.rs:47`: "stock dimensions exceed
  2000 mm", against a box the user stated in inches;
- machine limits - `machine/mod.rs:229,235,331`: "move 12 feeds 3000
  mm/min, X tops out at {ceiling}", a stated feed and a stated ceiling
  shown in a unit the document does not use;
- ui status and labels - `state.rs:2681` ("suggestion applied - 3180 rpm,
  480 mm/min"), `egui_app/feeds_page.rs:104` ("fz 0.050 mm"),
  `egui_app/setup_stock_pick.rs:69,72` (incoming-box range and `mm3`
  volume), `actions.rs:289,298` ("removed 12.500 mm3" beside a table that
  shows inches), `app/src/posting_sim.rs:60` ("worst 0.25 mm");
- generator refusals and notes - `operation/circle_fit.rs:67`,
  `operation/cross_stock.rs:282,301`, `operation/drill_reach.rs:71,169,194`,
  `operation/probe.rs:183`, `tool_body.rs:87,150`,
  `commands/cutting_data.rs:80`, `cutting.rs:199`.

The strings fall into two tiers, and they fix differently:

1. **Transient** - a status line, a refusal, a gate note, read once. These
   lens at the point they are built: `units::of(&world)` where the world is
   at hand, the pure `units::len/feed/area` formatters otherwise - they
   already exist and already do this job at the table edges.
   `geometry::units` has no volume formatter, so the `mm3` strings need one
   added there.
2. **Persisted into the document** - an op note, `path.notes`, the setup
   sheet, and from there the NC program header: `stock_sim.rs:523`,
   `commands/sync_stock.rs:181,183`, `operation/carried_stock.rs:215`. A
   lensed string frozen at generation time restates itself wrongly, because
   the unit is a lens that can flip after the generation. These want the
   structured-note pattern the sim warnings already use -
   `sim::verify::Warning` carries a number and the ui renders it through the
   lens (`sim_readout`) - so they are their own change.

Not reached by either: refusals whose `Display` lives in a crate with no
world (`tools/src/spun.rs:79,90`, `tools/src/holder_profile.rs:94`,
`tools/src/lathe_holder.rs:95-97`, `tools/src/lathe_insert_zone.rs:48`,
`motion/src/descent.rs:263`, `motion/src/probing.rs:149`) - lensing those
means plumbing `Unit` into the formatter itself.

**Adjacent, and a worse bug than this one, not part of it:** an inch machine
def's stated numbers are read as millimeters.
`assets/machines/tormach-pcnc440.mch` declares `"units": { "length": "inch" }`
with Z travel `-10.0..10.0`, and `machine::check_ops` compares program
coordinates, which are always millimeters, straight against those bands - a
mounted 440 refuses any move past 10 mm. Nothing converts a machine def's
numbers on read; there is no `MM_PER_INCH` in the machine reader.

**Done means:** the tier-1 strings render through the lens, pinned at app
and ui level, and `geometry::units` gains the volume formatter. The tier-2
notes stay frozen until the structured-note change.

Filed by an agent: `source:agent`, `P2`, `area:ui` - gh will not let a
non-member add labels, so they need applying by a member.

The machine limit check judges a touch probe's catalog `rpm` against the mounted machine's spindle range, so every probing program on a machine that states a minimum spindle speed is refused at post:

```
post blocked - machine Tormach 770MX: 1 limit problem(s): Probe X face: tool T99 Probe runs 1 rpm, below the machine's 175
```

Found while preparing the #521 hands-on probe test: catalog `PRB-0400` with the built-in Tormach 770MX (spindle 175-10000 rpm), Tormach PathPilot post.

**Cause:** `crates/app/src/machine/mod.rs` (~189-198) checks `tool.rpm` against `spindle_min`/`spindle_max` for every op, as the comment says ("today every op posts its tool's rpm"). A probe posts no speed at all: `posting.rs` forces rpm 0 for `ToolKind::Probe`, and #523/#526 posts no spindle start for it. So the probe's rpm field is never commanded, and judging it is a false refusal.

**Fix:** skip the spindle-range clause for probe tools (`ToolKind::Probe`), and for any op whose posted rpm is 0. Keep every other limit (axis travel, feeds) judged for probe moves.

Done means: a Probe op with the catalog probe posts on the Tormach 770MX (and any machine with a stated spindle minimum) with no limit problem, while a cutter below the minimum is still refused. Pinned by a machine-check test.

title: Locate the part in an imported fixture (or the fixture on the part) from the fixture and model pages

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-09: "we can import fixture. But we have no way of locating a part in the fixture on the fixture page or on the model page."

Part of #339 (fixtures/vises). Since #476/#549, a fixture's real mesh can be imported and is judged for collisions, but there's no way to put the part *in* it: the part and the fixture each sit where their files put them, so the collision verdict is only as good as that accidental placement.

**What's needed** (on the fixture page and the model page, the same tools both ways round):
1. **Mate by picks:** pick a face or point on the part, then the matching face or point on the fixture (a jaw face, a floor or parallel, a stop or locator pin). The part moves so the two coincide, with face normals opposed (part face sitting on the fixture face). Two or three mates fully locate it, the shop's 3-2-1 against a vise: the floor, the fixed jaw, then the stop.
2. **Numeric offset:** after a mate, nudge X/Y/Z (and a turn about the mate normal) by typed values. For example: 5 mm above the parallels, or 10 mm in from the stop.
3. **Move which one:** move the part into the fixture (default), or the fixture onto the part (common when the part is already aligned to the setup's plane, #330/#557, and the vise has to come to it).

**Rules:**
- **Commands:** every placement is one undoable command (`LocatePart` / `LocateFixture`), validated at creation and refused by name. That covers non-finite input, a degenerate pick (zero-area face, coincident points), a mate whose normals can't oppose, a placement that would leave the part interpenetrating the fixture (or at least warn by name), and no fixture or no model.
- **Frame:** the placement is relative to the setup the fixture belongs to. The setup's WCS (G54-G59, one per setup) is unchanged unless the user re-picks it. Stock follows the part as with part alignment (#326/#341).
- **Staleness:** moving the part or fixture marks that setup's ops stale (the collision verdict and toolpaths depend on it). Undo un-stales.
- **Shared code:** reuse the face/point pick from #554/#555/#557 so the setup and fixture tools share one picker, and the apply path from part alignment, so there's one transform model.

**Done means:**
- tests: a face mate sets the part's face coplanar with the fixture's, normals opposed; a 3-mate (floor, jaw, stop) gives a full location; a numeric offset moves the part exactly; LocateFixture moves the fixture, not the part; undo/redo walk each; degenerate picks are refused by name; the setup's ops go stale and the fixture collision check re-judges against the new placement.
- UI tests: the mate tools on the fixture page and the model page.

Related: #339, #476, #549 (fixture mesh and fixture UX), #330/#554/#555/#557 (alignment picks), #558 (WCS shown per setup).

title: Setup alignment: set the part's X and Y axis directions by picking an edge or two points

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Proposed by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-09: picking the "Y" axis by either an edge or two points, and then X as well, should be an option for aligning parts to the WCS.

**What:** a setup alignment mode that orients the part *within* the work plane, after (or independently of) laying it flat:
- **Y axis:** pick a straight edge, or two points; their direction becomes the setup's +Y (the user can flip the sense).
- **X axis:** the same, by an edge or two points. When both are picked, X is projected so X and Y stay perpendicular (Y wins, or the user picks which is primary; record the choice). When only one is picked, the other follows from the work-plane normal (right-handed: X = Y × Z).
- The axes are measured in the work plane (projected onto it), so a slightly tilted edge still gives a clean in-plane direction. A direction too close to the plane normal is refused by name.

**Relation to the other alignment work:**
- #330 (reopened): face to plane sets the *plane* (which way is down). This sets the *in-plane rotation* (which way X/Y point), so together they give a full part frame.
- #554 drops edge picking for *plane* alignment on the setup page, because an edge can't define a plane. Edges are valid here, because an edge does define a direction. The setup page should make clear which pick each mode takes (face for plane; edge or two points for an axis), so the face pick no longer fights edge snapping.
- #555: three points define a plane (and optionally a full frame from points 1 and 2). This mode can share its point-picking UI and apply path.
- The result applies to the part alignment (#326/#341) and leaves G54-G59 coming from the setup (one WCS per setup).

**Requirements:** one undoable command, validated at creation. Refused by name: a degenerate direction (zero length, two identical points), X and Y parallel, a direction along the plane normal, non-finite input. Undo restores the previous alignment.

**Done means:** tests for an edge at 30 degrees in the plane picked as Y rotating the part so that edge runs along +Y; two points picked as X doing the same for X; both picked giving perpendicular axes per the recorded rule; the degenerate and parallel cases refused by name; and undo/redo walking it.

title: Edge-break records have no upper bound on depth: a hand-edited project widens the forgiven band

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Follow-up from the review of PR #502 (#303).

`EdgeBreak::is_sane` (`crates/cl/src/cl/edge_break.rs`) and the project loader accept any finite, positive `depth`. The sim's edge-break credit (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/edge_break.rs`) forgives convicted columns down to `edge_z - depth + slope*d`, within the declared plan width. A record hand-edited (or corrupted) to a large depth therefore widens the band in which a real gouge is forgiven. Generated records are bounded by the operation's own parameters, so this only reaches a document through the file.

**Fix:** bound the record at load and in `is_sane`. The depth must not exceed the declaring operation's own chamfer/deburr depth (or a stated absolute cap, e.g. the tool's flute length), and the width must be consistent with the depth and slope. A record outside the bound is dropped by name, the same fail-closed path as a lattice mismatch: the program is then judged against the sharp model.

Done means: a project whose edge-break record states an inflated depth loads with that record dropped and a named note, and the program verdict convicts a cut below the operation's real depth. Pinned by a sim or app test.

Part of #303.

title: Align the model by picking a face or two edges onto a G17/G18/G19 plane

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Requested by the maintainer (2026-11-08), part of the setup/orientation problem: "a Face or two edges should be possible to locate to a G17-G19 plane as a shortcut to the turn and tilt offset functions - this is on the model."

## What
A one-click way to orient the **model** (not the work offset) by picking geometry:

- **Pick a planar face** -> choose a target plane: **G17 (XY)**, **G18 (ZX)** or **G19 (YZ)**. The model is rotated so that face lies on/parallel to the chosen plane, its outward normal along the plane's axis (+Z for G17, +Y for G18, +X for G19; a "flip" toggle for the opposite direction).
- **Pick two edges** (two non-parallel linear edges, or two coplanar edges) -> they define a plane the same way, and the first edge also fixes the rotation about the plane normal (it is laid along the plane's first axis: X for G17/G18, Y for G19).
- Optionally, place the result: snap the picked face onto the plane's level (e.g. face to Z=0) or keep the model's current position.

It is a shortcut for the existing turn/tilt (rotate model) functions: the same rotation, computed from the pick instead of typed angles.

## Where it fits
- It acts on the **model orientation** - the part's alignment. With #326 (per-setup part alignment to the setup's frame) it should write that setup's part alignment (so a second setup can lay a different face down); until #326 lands, it uses the document-level model transform (`MoveModel`).
- It does **not** rotate the work offset (that path is #187's 3-2-1, now refused when rotated by #315/PR #325) - program zero stays a plain translation (#196 / PR #328).

## Rules
- One undoable command (the same command the rotate/tilt functions use, with the computed rotation), written on command creation.
- Refuse by name: a non-planar face; two parallel or coincident edges, or a curved edge; a degenerate face; a pick on something that is not the model.
- Stock and toolpaths react as they do to a manual rotate today (stock re-fits if it is fitted to the model; operations go stale).

## Done means
Face -> G17/G18/G19 and two edges -> G17/G18/G19 both orient the model exactly (normal within a tight angular tolerance of the target axis; edge along the target axis), undo restores the previous orientation, the refusals fire by name, pinned by app tests (rotation math on known faces/edges of a fixture block and a tilted fixture) and a UI test of the pick flow.

Related: #326 (per-setup part alignment), #316 (transform between setups), #187 (3-2-1 work offset align), #315, #196 / PR #328, #308.

title: Documentation site: a docs folder published with GitHub Pages (user guide + architecture)
